extracted.intended_audience: students, poets, dramatists, and literary critics studying poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and criticizing poetry and dramatic works (especially tragedy and epic), focusing on plot, character, diction, and the elements that produce tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the principle of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation (mimesis) is the common principle of the arts of poetry, music, dancing, painting, and sculpture; they differ according to the medium, the objects, and the manner of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the medium (rhythm, language, harmony), the objects being imitated (higher or lower types), and the manner/form (dramatic, narrative, lyric). Use the appropriate medium and manner to suit the object you imitate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediums of imitation: rhythm, language, harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium of imitation is rhythm, language, and ‘harmony’ (melody), taken singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose which medium(s) to employ (e.g., dance uses rhythm; flute/lyre use harmony and rhythm; poetry uses language alone or combined). Match medium to the effect you intend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation — higher vs lower types
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher or lower types are represented in all the imitative arts; in poetry this distinction is the basis of the difference between Tragedy and Comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the work should portray elevated (tragic) or low/comic types; this choice affects tone, diction, and the moral evaluation of characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner/form of imitation (dramatic vs narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may be in form either dramatic narrative, pure narrative (including lyric), or pure drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an appropriate form (e.g., drama for immediate action and spectacle; epic/narrative for breadth and length) and be aware of how form shapes unity, length, and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six elements of Tragedy and relative priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy consists of six elements: three external—Spectacular Presentment (spectacle), Lyrical Song (choral odes), Diction; three internal—Plot, Character, and Thought. Plot is of primary importance; Character and Thought come next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In composing or evaluating tragedy, prioritize a well-constructed plot, then characterisation and intellectual content; avoid letting spectacle or mere diction overshadow plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole, complete, and of adequate magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot must be a Whole, complete in itself, and of adequate magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the action forms a unified whole with a beginning, middle, and end; the scale should be sufficient to sustain the plot's unity and tragic effect without extraneous material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Plot: unity of action not unity of hero
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Plot consists not in Unity of Hero, but in Unity of Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize incidents so they cohere to a single action or chain of events; avoid aggregating loosely related episodes merely because they share a protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic connection of parts and rule of sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts must be organically connected; incidents should follow by probable or necessary sequence rather than arbitrary juxtaposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply causes-and-effects logic (probability or necessity) to link scenes and events; resist episodic additions that break the causal chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic (universal) truth over historical (particular) truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic unity can be attained only by observance of Poetic as distinct from Historical Truth; poetry expresses the universal, history the particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to convey universal human truths and believable motivations rather than slavishly reporting particular facts; allow plausible generalization when it serves the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine the Inevitable and the Unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: The best Tragic effects depend on the combination of the Inevitable and the Unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure plot so outcomes feel both necessary in retrospect and yet surprising in their unfolding (e.g., foreshadowing that makes reversal psychologically inevitable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple plots and the value of reversal/recognition/pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex plots include reversal (peripeteia), recognition (anagnorisis), and suffering (pathos); such devices deepen tragic effect; simple plots lack these transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversal and recognition where organically motivated to intensify emotional impact; avoid contrived reversals or recognitions that violate probability or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quantitative parts (prologue, episode, choral ode)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has quantitative parts—Prologue, Episode, Chorus, etc.—which structure the dramatic action (some passages note these definitions may be later interpolations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange structural parts purposefully: prologue to prepare, episodes to advance action, choral odes to comment—make each part serve the unity of the plot rather than interrupt it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic action: change of fortune appropriate to character
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes Tragic Action: the change of fortune and the character of the hero are requisite to an ideal Tragedy; the unhappy ending is more truly tragic than poetic justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the protagonist's reversal arises from their nature and actions; a tragic downfall should evoke pity and fear grounded in character and circumstance, not arbitrary punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and fear must spring from the Plot itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic emotions of pity and fear should spring out of the Plot itself. To produce them by Scenery or Spectacular effect is entirely against the spirit of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elicit emotional responses through well-crafted incidents and character decisions; avoid relying on spectacle, stage effects, or sensationalism as substitutes for structural and moral causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as manifestation of moral purpose and rules for ethical portraiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is the manifestation of moral purpose; requisites of ethical portraiture include probability/necessity and suitability to the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create consistent, plausible characters whose choices follow from their dispositions; avoid characters acting in ways that contradict established traits merely to produce a plot twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Deus ex Machina (contrived solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Deus ex Machina' is criticized (passage notes as out of place); contrived interventions to resolve plot are to be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve complications through the logic of the plot and characters' actions rather than arbitrary external contrivances or sudden, unmotivated devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical craft rules for the tragic poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules: (1) To place the scene before his eyes, and to act the parts himself in order to enter into vivid sympathy with the dramatis personae. (2) To sketch the bare outline of the action before proceeding to fill in the episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imaginative embodiment and rehearsal to inhabit characters; plan the overall action (skeleton) first to maintain unity and avoid episodic drift when writing scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful handling of complication and denouement
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful about the Complication (dèlos) and Denouement (resolution) of the Plot, especially the Dénouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complications should arise naturally; the denouement must follow logically and provide a satisfying necessity rather than patching loose ends artificially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance forms of excellence and avoid epic overload
rubrics_metrics.description: To unite, if possible, varied forms of poetic excellence; not to overcharge a Tragedy with details appropriate to Epic Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate lyric, dramatic, and rhetorical strengths where organic, but do not borrow epic's long‑form detail that dilutes tragic concentration and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choral odes and other poetic elements must be organic
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the Choral Odes—like the Dialogue—an organic part of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure songs/choral passages advance theme, mood, or plot rather than serving as decorative interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought and diction: rhetoric and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (intellectual element) is revealed in dramatic speeches composed according to the rules of Rhetoric. Diction falls largely within the domain of the Art of Delivery rather than of Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft speeches that reveal thought via rhetorical techniques; match diction to character and situation, keeping delivery practical for actors/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction: admissible words, metaphors, elevation with perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic Diction: the words and modes of speech admissible in Poetry, including Metaphor. How Poetry combines elevation of language with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elevated language but maintain clarity; employ apt metaphors to illuminate character and action without obscuring meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy: differences in length, metre, and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic agrees with Tragedy in Unity of Action but differs in length, metre, and mode of delivering plausibility; epic's breadth can dilute concentrated tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose epic form for breadth and multiplicity of actions, tragedy for concentrated unity and intense emotional effect; do not try to graft epic scope onto tragic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to critical objections (impossible/irrational/morally hurtful/contradictory/artistic incorrectness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical objections fall into five sources: impossible, irrational, morally hurtful, contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness. Answers should be sought under the twelve heads previously enumerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending a poetic choice, justify apparent impossibilities by artistic requirements, poetic truth, or common opinion as appropriate; ensure choices obey internal necessity and ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth vs common reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic truth differs from common reality; poetry expresses the universal, and may employ probable or generalized truths rather than strict factual accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow plausibility and universality to guide representation; readers accept departures from literal fact if motivated by character, theme, or artistic necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing tragic effect to mere spectacle or bad acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive gesture or spectacle that compensates for lack of poetic construction is a fault; tragic art's power should exist even in reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on literary construction and character rather than extravagant histrionics; if action is used, it must be justified by the text and integrated into the plot.
